    "body": "Error Handling Design Category: Code | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Most systems get their error handling designed by accident: catch blocks appear where crashes were once observed, each with its own policy. This skill designs the failure path deliberately — classify errors by what recovery is possible, translate them at boundaries, and decide retry, fallback, or fail-fast where the context to decide actually lives. When to Use Use when designing or reviewing any module that can fail meaningfully — network calls, parsers, transactions, agents — especially where multiple layers could each independently retry or swallow errors. Do not catch broadly and continue; a swallowed error is a delayed failure with a lost cause. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The failing operations to design for | | | | Yes | Layer or system boundaries where errors translate | | | | Yes | Recovery rule per error class | Procedure 1. Enumerate the error classes per operation — transient, permanent, resource, integrity — before writing any handler; recovery decisions follow the class. 2. Fail fast on integrity and configuration errors; retrying a deterministic failure multiplies cost without changing the result. 3. Retry only transient errors, with backoff and a stated cap, and treat ambiguous outcomes as pending rather than failed. 4. Translate errors at boundaries: map internal classes to a documented contract with status, cause, and correlation id. 5. Attach context at the raise site — what ope ration, on what input class, at what stage — rather than reconstructing it later from strings. 6. Handle or propagate, and record which one happened where; an empty return after a caught error hides the failure from its caller. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Error classes, meanings, and boundary translations | | | | Recovery decisions per class with justification | | | | Correlation ids linking cause to observed failure | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Swallowed errors | Catch-all blocks continue with broken state | Handle or propagate; do not silently continue | | Retry everything | Deterministic failures retry to the cap | Classify before deciding recovery | | Lost cause chains | Context is stripped at the first boundary | Translate with cause and correlation id | | Empty returns after errors | Callers see empty results and no reason | Return the error or a documented default, with a record of which | | Boundary policy conflict | Two layers both retry, multiplying attempts | Decide retry ownership once per chain | Security and Authority Boundary Error messages are a disclosure channel: stack traces, query fragments, and file paths leak internals to callers and logs. When to Use - An agent needs code navigation, diagnostics, refactoring, or test feedback that is stronger than raw terminal/file operations. - An IDE exposes structured APIs that can reduce brittle text-based interaction. - Multiple coding agents or models must use the same IDE capability boundary. - An agent should receive compiler, linter, test, or inspection feedback immediately after a change. - You need explicit permission boundaries around IDE actions such as running commands, debugging, or mutating project state.     "body": "Mutation Testing Category: Code | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Coverage says a line ran; it does not say anyone would notice if it were wrong. Mutation testing flips the question: introduce small, mechanical changes to the code — flip a comparison, drop a call — and check whether the test suite fails. Surviving mutants are lines the suite does not actually defend, and each one is a concrete, fixable gap. When to Use Use when a suite has high coverage but defects still escape — release-critical libraries, parser cores, financial logic — and the question is whether the tests assert real behavior. Do not run mutation testing over an entire large codebase at once; it multiplies suite runtime by the mutant count, so scope it to critical modules. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The module under assessment | | | | Yes | The test suite to measure | | | | No | Mutation operators to apply; default set | Procedure 1. Select the scope deliberately — critical modules first — because every mutant costs a full suite run. 2. Apply mutations one at a time: small, mechanical edits such as flipping an operator, changing a constant, or removing a call. 3. Run the suite per mutant and record the result: killed, survived, or timed out. 4. Treat timeouts as kills only when the suite is deterministic; flaky suites make mutation results noise. 5. Group surviving mutants and convert each group into a missing assertion or a new test that kills it. 6. Re-run and compare the mutat ion score — the fraction killed — instead of trusting coverage alone.     "id": "05-code/property-based-testing",
    "title": "Property Based Testing",
    "category": "05-code",
    "level": "intermediate",
    "stability": "experimental",
    "tags": [],
    "description": "Test executable invariants over generated inputs instead of fixed examples, then shrink failing cases toward minimal counterexamples that reproduce the defect with the least context.",
    "body": "Property Based Testing Category: Code | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Example-based tests check the cases someone thought of; property-based tests state invariants and let a generator search the input domain for violations. When a generated case fails, shrinking reduces it toward the smallest reproducer, which becomes the bug report and a permanent regression test. This skill covers that loop — declare invariants, generate, shrink, repair — as a reviewable engineering procedure. When to Use Use when a function or service has a checkable invariant over a wide input space and hand-written examples cover only a thin slice of it. Do not use for exact-output specifications or UI flows; deterministic example tests fit those better. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Predicates that must hold for every generated input | | | | Yes | Input-domain definitions including edge cases | | | | No | Maximum shrinking steps per counterexample | | | | No | Deterministic seed for reproducible runs | Procedure 1. State each invariant as a predicate over generated inputs; an invariant that cannot be phrased as a predicate is a smell. 2. Define the input domain explicitly, including boundaries: empty, zero, negative, and maximum-shaped cases. 3. Run generated cases against each invariant and collect every failing input. 4. Shrink each failing input toward a minimal reproducer; the shrunk case is what gets reported. 5. Pin the shrunk counterexample as a permanent deterministic example test. 6. Repair the defect, re-run the full property, and only then remove any temporary filters. 7. Rotate seeds on a schedule; a fixed seed set forever is just a slow example suite. 8. Record which invariants ran; an unexercised invariant is untested behavior. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Generated inputs that violated an invariant | | | | Minimal reproducers suitable for regression tests | | | | Pass or fail state per declared invariant | | | | Number of generated cases executed | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Weak invariant | The property restates the implementation | Derive invariants from the specification, not the code | | No shrinking | The first random failure is reported as-is | Shrink tow ard minimal inputs before reporting | | Shrunk-case loss | The counterexample is never pinned | Add the shrunk case as a deterministic regression test | | Fixed-seed blindness | The same seed runs forever | Rotate seeds while keeping failures reproducible | | Generator gaps | The domain excludes edge values | Include empty, zero, negative, and maximum cases | Security and Authority Boundary Property-based testing grants no authority to run generated inputs against production systems. Generators produce untrusted data: targets under test must be sandboxed, and shrinking must never reduce toward inputs that trigger real side effects.     "body": "Static Analysis Category: Code | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Static analysis reads code the way a reviewer with infinite patience would: every path, every assignment, every tainted flow from input to dangerous sink. Its problem is signal — tools over-report, and untriaged findings train teams to ignore them. This skill covers configuring analyzers, triaging output honestly, and maintaining a rule inventory that documents why each rule earns its noise. When to Use Use as a continuous gate on changed code and as a periodic deep pass — taint analysis on untrusted-input paths, security rules on everything that handles data. Do not run analyzers in default configuration over legacy code and report thousands of findings at once; that output gets archived rather than acted on. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The codebase or module to analyze | | | | Yes | Rule set and severity thresholds in force | | | | No | Previously triaged and waived findings | Procedure 1. Configure a profile for the codebase: enabled rules, severities, and the reasoning that each noisy rule is worth its cost. 2. Analyze the whole program where the tool supports it — cross-function taint paths die at file scope. 3. Triage every finding against the baseline: confirm, waive with a reason, or fix now; never leave untriaged findings in the gate. 4. Distinguish findings by kind — real defect, style preference, false positive — and adjust rules to shrink the third category. 5. Feed confirmed security findings to the defect queue with the taint path attached, not just the line number. 6. Re-baseline after fixes: the baseline records what was consciously accepted, not what was ignored.     "description": "Emit logs as structured events — timestamp, level, ids, and measured fields — with stable schemas, correlation ids, and redaction rules instead of free-text lines.",
    "body": "Structured Logging Category: Code | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A log line that only a human can parse is a cost center: it cannot be filtered, alerted on, or audited at scale. Structured logging emits events — a stable name, a level, a timestamp, and measured fields — with correlation ids that tie each event to the request or agent step that produced it, and redaction rules that keep sensitive values out of records by design. When to Use Use whenever more than one system or more than one day separates writing from reading — services, pipelines, agent frameworks — where logs must be filtered by field rather than grepped by hope. Do not log raw payloads as fields; structure exists partly to make redaction enforceable. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The operations to instrument | | | | Yes | Field names and types per event | | | | No | Fields to drop or mask at emit time | Procedure 1. Define the event vocabulary first — a stable event name per operation, with a documented field schema per event. 2. Include correlation ids in every event: request id, run id, step id, so a chain is reconstructable across systems. 3. Emit at the level that matches the reader: debug for development detail, info for operations, warning for degraded-but-serving, error for failures with an owner. 4. Redact by schema rather than by review: sensitive fields are masked or dropped at emit time, before any sink sees them. 5. Measure rather than narrate: durations, counts, and statuses as typed fields, with free text as a supplement rather than the record. 6. Log an error once with full context at the handling site, not re-logged at every layer of propagation.
